newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Minority Indonesian party calls for basic rights.
newsitem.headline: Minority Indonesian party calls for basic rights.

text.p: Indonesia's minority Moslem-oriented party opened its campaign on Sunday for May 29 general elections with a pledge to fight for four basic rights for the country's 200 million people.

United Development Party (PPP) chief Ismail Hasan Metareum called at a rally of about 5,000 people in the north Sumatran trading centre of Medan for the right to education, political activity, security and work.
"These four are essential rights of the people," he said. "The PPP will fight constitutionally for these rights."

The PPP, which won 17 percent of the vote in the last elections in 1992, the ruling Golkar and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) are the only three political groups legally allowed to contest the elections.
Nearly 125 million people are entitled to vote for the 425 elected seats in the 500-member House of Representatives. The other 75 seats are allotted to the military, which does not vote.
The three parties have agreed to campaign in separate areas each day in the month-long campaign in a bid to avoid violence between rival supporters.
The PPP was campaigning on Sunday on Sumatra, the resort island of Bali and the adjacent islands of Nusa Tenggara.

Hundreds of youths, some with their heads shaved in the form of the party's star symbol or to represent three Ps, roamed Medan on motorcycles before the afternoon rally shouting "Hidup Bintang (Long live the star)".

Ismail Hasan told Reuters in an interview that he expected the PPP to win up to 100 seats in parliament, compared with 62 in 1992 and a peak of 99 in 1977. Golkar won 68 percent of the vote and 282 seats in 1992 and the PDI 56 seats and 15 percent.
Other senior PPP leaders were not so optimistic as Ismail Hasan.

"The PPP has difficulties under this system," said party MP Bachtiar Chamsyah. "We are caught between the bureaucracy and the Golkar cadres. In the rural areas, the leader of each village is usually a Golkar man and he controls the polling.
"A sense of unfairness is affecting the PPP," he said.

Medan was peaceful on Sunday but police said three PPP supporters were slightly hurt in a scuffle with Golkar members on Saturday night as both sides put up campaign flags. The three went home after first aid treatment.

Although some 80 percent of Indonesians are Moslems, no political party can use religious appeals in its campaign. All three parties have sworn to uphold the Pancasila ideology, which recognises the five main religions.
